newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson says premature to raise Great Western bid.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson says premature to raise Great Western bid.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. executives Monday blasted Washington Mutual Inc.'s $6.6 billion merger agreement with Great Western Financial Corp., saying it would hurt rather than help earnings.
"The transaction (proposed by Washington Mutual) is dilutive without the revenue enhancements they claim," said Ahmanson Chief Financial Officer Kevin Twomey during a meeting with analysts.
Twomey said Washington Mutual's projections were "highly aggressive" and said Washington Mutual's claims to cut costs and raise revenues with its acquisition of Great Western were unattainable.

"No one has ever attempted to do that before and for the simple reason that the two are incompatible," Twomey said, A Great Western spokesman said Ahmanson's presentation "was a desperate and hollow attempt to justify what continues to be an inferior merger proposal and a losing proposition.
"We remain committed to the agreement with (WAMU) and we're confident it will be consummated quickly," he said.
The spokesman said Washington Mutual will be able to answer Ahmanson's claims more directly after it makes a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission later this week.
Ahmanson Chief Executive Charles Rinehart said his company's $6.1 billion bid for Great Western was financially superior to the deal reached between Great Western and Washington Mutual.

Rinehart also indicated that full-year estimates for Ahmanson are likely to top analysts' estimates by 5 percent to 15 percent. Analysts' consensus for the full year is for Ahmanson to earn $2.96 per share.

"I think they did a good job," said David Hochstim, analyst with Bear Stearns, adding, "they indicated that consensus estimates for Ahmanson alone were too low by 10 percent, which implies they'll have higher earnings for the next few years on a standalone basis and combined with Great Western if they are sucessful."
Hochstim said it was too early in the takeover battle to predict which thrift would emerge the winner.
Ahmanson surprised Great Western in February with a hostile takeover. However, Great Western chose to seek a friendlier deal with Washington Mutual, sparking a bitter exchange between the two banks.
Campbell Chaney, analyst with Sandler O'Neill said he expected more mudslinging and jawboning was expected from both sides in coming weeks.
"It's kind of a waiting game. It's going to come down to a shareholder vote and its a necessary procedure for each side to sell their deal," said Chaney.

Meanwhile, Ahmanson's presentation did not show immediate results as the value of its bid to exchange 1.05 of its shares for Great Western shares, slid to $44.25 a share Monday from $44.50 a share on Friday. Washington Mutual's offer to exchange 0.9 of its shares for each Great Western share actually rose in value to $48.94 a share Monday from $47.59 a share on Friday.

Several analysts have said that Ahmanson needs to raise its offer to remain a contender. "If the gap keeps growing wider in the next several weeks in favor of Washington Mutual, then Amhanson will have to increase its bid," Chaney said.
Ahmanson indicated it might raise the bid, but not by much.
"We're committed to getting this deal done ... but only to the extent that we think the economics make sense," Rinehart said in response to questions about Ahmanson's next move.

A Washington Mutual-Great Western merger would create the nation's largest savings and loan with $87.4 billion in assets. Ahmanson would strengthen its position as the largest thrift if it bought Great Western.

Rinehart labeled Washington Mutual's merger plan a "hope and pray" strategy, saying Seattle-based Washington Mutual was hoping to get aggressive cost savings and would "pray for a miracle on the revenue side."
Analysts have said Ahmanson should be able to achieve more cost savings than Washington Mutual because both Ahmanson and Great Western are based in southern California.

Rinehart said that if Ahmanson prevailed in a lawsuit seeking to overturn a "breakup fee" in the merger pact between Washington Mutual and Great Western, the money would go to the best interests of shareholders.
The Washington Mutual bid calls for it to collect up to $195 million if the deal breaks up and Great Western merges with someone else within 18 months.
Washington Mutual Chief Executive Kerry Killinger said last week that his company's earnings would be boosted by a merger with Great Western.
Rinehart said Ahmanson's plan for Great Western relied on a "simple and proven formula:" taking cost savings, generating more capital and using the excess to repurchase stock.

He said Washington Mutual was "stretching the envelope" with its projection of $340 million in cost savings in 1999 in a merger with Great Western. Ahmanson has said its proposed merger with Great Western would save $400 million a year.
